_comment: Everything deployment-specific for watchdog.py. The script names no session,
path or person - point STALL_WATCHDOG_CONFIG at a copy to run a second setup.
This watchdog answers a blocking confirmation prompt that nobody is present to
answer. It ALWAYS answers no. See SKILL.md for why that is the only safe
automatic answer.
The session to watch. TMUX_TMPDIR must match the one the session was created
with, or tmux will not find it and every capture fails with 'no server running'.
The service unit sets TMUX_TMPDIR=/run/claude-tmux-<agent>; this must agree.
stall_secs 120: a prompt must sit UNCHANGED for two minutes before it is answered.
⚠️ This is deliberately SHORT. It assumes nobody is at the terminal. If a human is present and reading a prompt, they have two minutes to
answer before it is refused for them. Raise it if that stops being true.
⚠️ BOTH conditions must hold before acting: a prompt signature matches AND the
pane has not changed for stall_secs. The unchanged test alone is meaningless -
a session idling at its input prompt is unchanged for hours and that is its
normal resting state. The signature alone would answer a prompt someone is
actively reading. Requiring both is what keeps Escape away from real work.
prompt_patterns are matched against the captured pane, MULTILINE. ANY hit means
'a prompt is on screen'. Keep them SPECIFIC to the confirmation UI: a false
positive sends Escape into whatever the session is genuinely doing, while a false
negative only leaves the stall for a human. Only the first can destroy work.
⚠️ The first pattern matches the SELECTION CURSOR - '❯' then a number then a dot -
and deliberately does NOT match the option text. Option names vary by dialog:
Yes/No for a command confirmation, but Compact, Login and others elsewhere. Keying
on 'Yes|No' silently missed every dialog that was not a command confirmation.
The cursor is the one element common to all of them.
The '❯' alone is NOT enough: it is also the session's own input prompt, which is
on screen whenever the agent is idle. Requiring a digit and a dot after it is what
separates a chooser from the resting state - get this wrong and the watchdog
Escapes an idle session every stall_secs, forever.
These patterns ARE verified against a real captured prompt - see the
fixtures/real-prompt-*.txt files, consecutive tmux captures taken while a
genuine confirmation was on screen. All three match them.
The captured prompt is Claude Code's 'Dangerous rm operation on
possibly-empty variable path' guard; what trips it is technical/watchdog.md
section 5. The patterns do not depend on why a prompt was raised: they are
tested against real captures of one that appeared.
A SECOND real pair, fixtures/real-prompt-permission-{a,b}.txt, captures an ordinary
Bash PERMISSION confirmation - the class this watchdog actually targets, and unlike
the rm guard it can be raised again on demand. All three patterns hit it, and
watchdog.test.py section 2c asserts each one individually so a pattern that stops
covering this dialog class cannot hide behind the other two.
To re-verify after any UI change: run 'watchdog.py --probe' while a prompt is
on screen. It reports which patterns hit and which miss, and takes no action.
prompt_patterns: Esc to cancel · Tab to amend
_idle_comment: ⚠️ THE EXCLUSION MATTERS MORE THAN THE PATTERNS. The pane being read also shows
the agent's OWN commands and output - so an agent that prints, greps or edits
text containing a chooser (the watchdog's own config and tests do exactly that)
would otherwise detect itself as prompting, and be Escaped stall_secs later while
perfectly healthy: a test run printing sample dialogs matches the live pane -
measured.
The discriminator is structural, not textual. A modal dialog REPLACES the input
box and status bar at the foot of the pane. Idle or working, they are always
there; while a dialog is up they are always gone. So if the LAST idle_tail_lines
carry the idle signature, it is not a prompt - regardless of what is on screen
further up. Text can be quoted; the structure cannot.
idle_tail_lines 6: the input box, its two rules and the status bar. Large enough
to catch them, small enough that a dialog's own footer never reaches back into it.
⚠️ THESE PATTERNS ARE PERMISSION-MODE SPECIFIC, WHICH IS NOT OBVIOUS AND HAS NO
SIGNAL. '⏵⏵' is carried by the auto and accept-edits status bars. A session cycled
to MANUAL or PLAN mode shows '⏸ manual mode on · ? for shortcuts · ← for agents' or
'⏸ plan mode on (shift+tab to cycle) · ← for agents', and NONE of these three
patterns matches either - measured. The exclusion then reads INERT on a perfectly
healthy session, which --probe reports and nothing else does. Re-check with --probe
against a session in the mode it will actually run in, not the mode it starts in.
_comment_known_prompts: Prompts the watchdog is TAUGHT to answer, tried in order and checked BEFORE the
generic Escape-the-prompt fallback. Each entry needs: name, match (regex searched
against the whole pane), keys (sent via tmux send-keys, in order), notice.
⚠️ NEVER add an entry whose correct answer you are not certain of. The default
refusal is safe precisely because it is uninformed; a wrong CHOICE can be much
worse than a refusal. The entry below is the case in point: which resume option
is right is a deployment decision, and each choice costs something - compacting
discards session context on every unattended restart, and resuming in full
reloads whatever state the session stopped in.
⚠️ Still no 'approve' for permission prompts, and there must never be one. These
entries are for NON-permission prompts that block start-up - a different class.

known_prompts.name: claude-code-resume-return
known_prompts.match: Resuming the full session will consume a substantial portion
known_prompts.notice: WATCHDOG: the Claude Code session-resume prompt blocked start-up for {duration}. It answered 'Resume full session as-is' - NOT compact. ⚠️ Which option this answers is a deployment decision: compacting on every unattended restart silently discards session context. Nothing else was done. ⚠️ No Monitors are running: re-arm the monitors your charter names, now, per its start-up list.
_comment: Options, in the order the binary declares them: [compact] 'Resume from summary
(recommended)', [continue] 'Resume full session as-is', [never] "Don't ask me
again". The first is preselected, so Down+Enter selects the second.
⚠️ CONTINUE vs a fresh session is a DEPLOYMENT DECISION, not a default. The
keys below resume the full session, which keeps the detail compaction loses;
record your own choice in the install's CONTEXT.md.
Relative navigation rather than a digit key, because it does not assume the
chooser is numbered - and the digit would be wrong if the list ever reorders.
⚠️ This should never fire. resumeReturnDismissed:true in <the session's CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR>/.claude.json
suppresses the prompt outright; this is the backstop for a config reset, which
matters because that file is harness-managed state, not maintained config.
deny_key is the keystroke that REFUSES. In Claude Code's confirmation UI the
'No, and tell Claude what to do differently' option is bound to Escape.
⚠️ There is deliberately no 'approve' option in this file and there must never
be one. Auto-approving would defeat a guard that exists for a reason, and would
do it with nobody watching.
notice is injected into the session AFTER the refusal lands. It must say that
the refusal was mechanical: an agent that believes a considered decision was
made on its behalf will not revisit it, and the whole point is that it should.
action.notice: WATCHDOG: you entered a stall - a confirmation prompt sat unanswered for {duration} because nobody is at this terminal. The watchdog answered NO on your behalf, without thinking: it has no idea whether no was the right answer, it only knows that hanging forever is worse. Your command was refused, not executed. Re-read what you were about to run, decide whether it actually needs doing, and if it does, find a route that does not trip the guard. Then tell whoever was waiting what happened.

_comment: Cursor and single-instance lock. ⚠️ Never read this from an environment
variable: that makes the location a property of whoever launched the process,
and a launcher that differs gets its own lock and runs a second watchdog
alongside the first - two processes racing to Escape the same prompt.
Only this CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR may run the watchdog; anyone else exits 0 with a
WATCHDOG-GUARD line. Left null when run from systemd, which has no
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR set and is the intended launcher - the flock is the real
single-instance guard.
